sources.title: The Bootstrap Method for Assessing Statistical Accuracy
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 35 PDF pages and printed pages 1–35, §§1–10, including examples, interval discussions, Monte Carlo sample-size section and jackknife/delta-method section.
anchors: §§1–2, printed pp. 1–3: empirical-distribution plug-in, bootstrap standard error and basic IID setup.
§§3–6, printed pp. 4–21: examples, bias/prediction error and more complicated sampling structures including regression, censoring and time series.
§§7–8, printed pp. 22–29: standard, percentile, BC/BCa and multiparameter interval discussion.
§9, printed pp. 29–30: finite bootstrap sample size and Monte Carlo error.
§10, printed pp. 30–32: delete-one jackknife, delta method and nonsmooth-statistic caveats.
Appendix program and references, printed pp. 33–35.
claims_and_hypotheses: The standard empirical bootstrap samples IID from the empirical distribution; alternative data structures need a resampling design that matches their sampling units/dependence.
Bias, prediction error and interval procedures are described; BC/BCa claims require regularity conditions and the article omits most formal proofs.
The jackknife approximates bootstrap variance for smooth statistics through a first-order linearization; median/nonsmooth behavior is a failure case.
Finite-B bootstrap error is Monte Carlo error conditional on the observed dataset and is distinct from sampling error.
sources.proof_status: Invited review/tutorial. The article explicitly omits most proofs and directs readers particularly to Efron (1982). It is not recorded as proof of its general bootstrap or BCa claims.
limitations: Not a theorem proving generic bootstrap validity.
Higher-order interval claims are presented with references/examples rather than full proofs in this article.
sources.rights_note: The publisher page records a 2021 retrospective open-access correction/order. The private ignored cache is not redistributed.

sources.title: Resampling Fewer Than n Observations: Gains, Losses, and Remedies for Losses
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 31 PDF pages and printed pages 1–31, including the appendix proofs.
anchors: §1, printed pp. 1–4: motivation and bootstrap failure examples.
§2, printed pp. 4–8: failure modes including extremes, nonsmooth and degenerate statistics.
§3 and Theorems 1–3, printed pp. 8–14: m-out-of-n with replacement/without replacement and sample splitting.
§§4–6 and Theorem 4/propositions, printed pp. 14–21: relative efficiency and extrapolation conditions.
§§7–8 and Appendix proofs, printed pp. 21–31.
claims_and_hypotheses: IID base sample; m-out-of-n schemes with m→∞ and m/n→0 can be first-order valid under the stated root/distribution conditions.
Theorems distinguish with-replacement bootstrap, without-replacement subsampling, and sample-splitting.
Second-order extrapolation is justified only when the ordinary bootstrap already works and the expansion assumptions hold; it need not repair irregular cases.
sources.proof_status: Theorems and their article-local proofs were read. Higher-order claims retain the stated differentiability/expansion conditions.
limitations: Choosing m is difficult and no universal data-independent choice is supplied.
IID results should not be transferred to dependent time series without a separate dependence theorem.

sources.title: On the Uniform Asymptotic Validity of Subsampling and the Bootstrap
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 25 PDF pages and journal pages 2798–2822. Read the main proofs in Appendix A.1–A.2, including the core subsampling and bootstrap quantile-validity arguments.
anchors: §2.1/Theorem 2.1, PDF pp. 4–6 / journal pp. 2801–2803: subsampling, b→∞, b/n→0, one-sided and two-sided uniform CDF conditions.
§2.2/Theorems 2.2–2.4, PDF pp. 6–10 / journal pp. 2803–2807: feasible roots, studentization and bootstrap distribution approximation.
§3, PDF pp. 10–20 / journal pp. 2807–2817: applications to means, inequalities, multiple testing, empirical processes and U-statistics.
Appendix A.1–A.2, PDF pp. 21–25 / journal pp. 2818–2822: proofs of main Theorems 2.1 and 2.4.
claims_and_hypotheses: Uniform coverage requires distribution-class uniformity, not merely pointwise weak convergence.
Subsampling uses b→∞, b/n→0 and uniform one-/two-sided approximation of the root's CDF; feasible roots need their own uniform approximation condition.
Bootstrap validity requires a suitable estimated-distribution metric together with uniform stability of the target root law; weak-metric closeness alone need not control quantiles.
sources.proof_status: Main theorem proofs in the article were read. Proofs of some application results are delegated to the supplementary material and were not read; those applications are not used as proved dependencies.
limitations: Uniform conditions can be strong and must be verified over the stated class P.
The supplementary application proofs are outside the cached/read artifact.

sources.title: Moving Block and Tapered Block Bootstrap for Functional Time Series with an Application to the K-Sample Mean Problem
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of the cached arXiv v3 main article, all 29 PDF pages, including its appendix and displayed proofs. The separately referenced supplementary file was not available.
anchors: §2.1/Assumption 1, PDF pp. 2–3: strictly stationary L2-valued process, L2-m-approximability and strengthened approximation rate.
§2.2/Theorem 2.1, PDF pp. 4–6: moving-block bootstrap sample-mean law and long-run covariance consistency.
§2.3/Theorem 2.2, PDF pp. 6–7: tapered-block bootstrap statement and window assumptions.
§3/Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.1, PDF pp. 7–13: null-centered multi-series functional mean tests and continuous-statistic transfer.
§5/Appendix, PDF pp. 16–27: Lemma 5.1 and MBB/Theorem 2.1/3.1 proofs; the article states Lemma 5.2 and TBB/Theorem 2.2 proofs are in the supplement.
claims_and_hypotheses: Strictly stationary L2-valued series satisfying the paper's exact L2-m-approximability Assumption 1.
Block length satisfies b^-1 + b n^-1/2 = o(1). The TBB additionally requires the stated data-tapering window conditions.
For two independent series, min(n1,n2)→∞, n1/(n1+n2)→theta in (0,1), and each block size satisfies the source rate.
Testing theorem applies to continuous functionals of the stated deviation process; it is not a theorem for every possible test statistic.
sources.proof_status: Main article and MBB proofs read. The source explicitly defers the proof of Lemma 5.2 and TBB Theorem 2.2 to an online supplement; that proof was not read.
limitations: The paper relies on a separate Hilbert-valued FCLT for the original sample mean.
Block-length rate is asymptotic and does not solve finite-sample block selection.
Only the stated L2-m-approximable functional-time-series setting is covered.

supplement_attempt.additional_check: Downloaded/listed the arXiv v3 source archive; it contains MBB-TBB-Rev.tex and example PDFs, not the supplementary proof file.

sources.title: A Survey of Cross-Validation Procedures for Model Selection
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 40 PDF pages and journal pages 40–79.
anchors: §§1–3, journal pp. 40–51: statistical framework, risk versus identification goals, model-selection procedures.
§4, journal pp. 51–56: holdout, LOO, LPO, V-fold and repeated CV definitions.
§5, journal pp. 57–61: risk-estimator bias and variance.
§§6–7, journal pp. 61–65: efficient selection and identification/model-consistency conditions.
§8, journal pp. 66–68: density, outliers, time-series dependence and many-model cases.
§9 onward, journal pp. 69–79: computational formulas, bibliography and conclusion.
claims_and_hypotheses: CV risk estimation and model identification/selection are distinct targets.
Risk-estimation bias depends on training size; overlapping folds induce correlated errors and a variance/bias/cost tradeoff.
The survey separates rigorous results from empirical observations; it gives no universally best K.
Dependent data need a matching split strategy; IID CV justifications do not transfer automatically.
sources.proof_status: The full survey was read. It summarizes many results and explicitly distinguishes source proofs from empirical evidence; it is not itself a complete proof for every cited framework.
limitations: Model-selection results are setting-specific; do not universalize one V-fold conclusion.
CV estimates prediction risk at its training size, not automatically the risk of a full-data refit.

sources.title: No Unbiased Estimator of the Variance of K-Fold Cross-Validation
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 17 PDF pages and journal pages 1089–1105, including the proof of Theorem 6.
anchors: §§2.1–2.5, journal pp. 1090–1094: performance estimands, holdout, K-fold and alternative CV estimators.
§3 and Lemma 1/Corollaries 2–3, journal pp. 1094–1097: covariance matrix with three eigenvalue components and variance decomposition.
§4, Lemmas 4–8 and Theorem 6, journal pp. 1097–1102: no universal unbiased variance estimator and proof.
§§5–6, journal pp. 1102–1105: examples, simulation and conclusion.
claims_and_hypotheses: Symmetric learning algorithm, IID data and the stated fixed K-fold design.
K-fold errors have dependence from overlapping training sets; their covariance matrix has three distinct covariance/eigenvalue components.
Theorem 6 rules out a universal unbiased estimator over all distributions under the paper's setup; it does not rule out model-specific or biased/asymptotic estimates.
sources.proof_status: The full theorem proof was read. The paper's universal quantifier and fixed K-fold scope are retained.
limitations: The result is not an impossibility theorem for every CV variance estimator under every model.
An independent holdout design has a different covariance structure.

sources.title: Asymptotically Valid and Exact Permutation Tests Based on Two-Sample U-Statistics
sources.publication: Stanford Statistics Technical Report 2011-09 (October 2011), 47-page cached PDF; later journal article in Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 168 (2016), 97–105.
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 47 PDF pages, including the main theorem proofs and appendices.
anchors: §2/Theorems 2.1–2.3, PDF pp. 12–19: Wilcoxon parameter theta=P(X≤Y), studentization and exactness under P=Q.
§3/Theorems 3.1–3.2, PDF pp. 20–26: antisymmetric two-sample U-statistic extension.
Appendices A–B, PDF pp. 35–47: projection, permutation approximation and proof details.
claims_and_hypotheses: Independent samples, IID within P and Q; sample proportions converge to p in (0,1).

Studentized Wilcoxon-type test controls asymptotic size for the weak parameter null theta(P)=theta(Q)=1/2 under continuity/variance and consistency assumptions, while it is finite-sample exact under P=Q.
General U-statistic extension requires the source's antisymmetric kernel, finite moments, positive limiting variance and consistent variance estimates.
The report proves a narrower U-statistic class than the 2013 asymptotically-linear generalization.
sources.proof_status: Full report proof read. This is the independent proof basis for the proposed U-statistic interface.
limitations: Does not license unstudentized tests under a weak parameter null.
Does not replace the 2013 supplement proof for the broader asymptotically-linear/k-sample result.

sources.title: Exact Testing with Random Permutations
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 15 PDF pages and TEST pages 811–825, including proofs.
anchors: Theorem 1 and proof, pp. 813–815: finite-group exact/conservative tests and tie handling.
Theorem 2 and proof, pp. 816–819: random transformations, identity inclusion and weak validity.
Propositions 1–3, pp. 814–821: exactness conditions and randomized boundary variants.
Discussion and references, pp. 822–825.
claims_and_hypotheses: Finite group action and invariance of the null law are essential.
Full-group rank tests are conservative under ties; randomized tie breaking can produce exact level.
Random-permutation correction with the identity is weakly valid under the source's transformation-sampling conditions; an uncorrected B/w can be anti-conservative or zero.
sources.proof_status: Theorem and proposition proofs were read in the article.
limitations: Exact group-invariance testing is not automatically a treatment-assignment test; use the actual design distribution for randomization inference.
Random transformations do not make a non-invariant null invariant.

sources.title: Multilevel Monte Carlo Path Simulation
sources.read_status: Complete full-text read of all 11 PDF pages and journal pages 607–617, including Theorem 3.1 and its proof.
anchors: §§1–2, pp. 607–609: standard MC MSE and the telescoping coupled-level estimator.
§3/Theorem 3.1 and proof, pp. 609–611: abstract bias/variance/cost exponents and complexity regimes.
§§4–5, pp. 611–613: level selection, Richardson extrapolation and the explicitly heuristic adaptive algorithm.
§6–7, pp. 613–617: numerical examples, limitations and concluding discussion.
claims_and_hypotheses: The theorem assumes weak-bias exponent alpha≥1/2, correction-variance exponent beta>0 and level cost proportional to N_l h_l^-1.
Fine/coarse approximations are coupled through the same Brownian path within a level; estimators are independent across levels.
For alpha=1, beta=1, complexity is O(epsilon^-2 log(epsilon)^2); standard Euler MC is O(epsilon^-3).
For discontinuous payoffs the source gives a correction-variance rate beta=1/2 under its cited SDE assumptions, yielding O(epsilon^-5/2).
sources.proof_status: The abstract multilevel complexity theorem and proof are complete in the article. The SDE weak/strong convergence facts used in applications are cited, not proved here.
limitations: The theorem's constants/rates are assumed known; the adaptive bias-stopping procedure is explicitly heuristic and not guaranteed.
No general MLMC plus QMC complexity proof is included.

sources.title: Monte Carlo Book: the Quasi-Monte Carlo Parts
sources.publication: Author manuscript dated July 2019, Chapters 15–17, pp. 3–138.
sources.read_status: Complete assigned chapters 15–17: printed pp. 3–138, PDF pp. 5–140. Read all chapter prose, formulas, theorem statements, proof discussions, examples and captions. The PDF title/contents pages and bibliography beyond the assigned chapters are not claimed as a full bibliography reading. Raw plot glyphs were not visually audited; captions and surrounding analysis were read.
anchors: Chapter 15, printed pp. 3–60 / PDF pp. 5–62: discrepancy, Riemann-integrable convergence, Koksma–Hlawka, van der Corput/Halton, digital nets, projections, infinite variation and higher-order nets.
Chapter 16, printed pp. 61–88 / PDF pp. 63–90: rank-one lattices, Fourier criteria, periodizing transformations, convergence rates, embedded/extensible lattices and weighted spaces.

Chapter 17, printed pp. 89–138 / PDF pp. 91–140: RQMC definition, Cranley–Patterson rotation, scrambled nets, replicate variance/error estimates, singular integrands, effective dimension, hybrids/Latin supercube, array-RQMC, and the bootstrap-t end note at printed pp. 132–134.
claims_and_hypotheses: Koksma–Hlawka requires finite Hardy–Krause variation and a discrepancy bound; it is deterministic and generally not an operational confidence interval.
RQMC unbiasedness follows from uniform marginal points; independent full-rule randomizations support between-replicate variance estimation.
Nested uniform scramble results have explicit base/net and smoothness assumptions; general finite-variance bounds and smooth fast rates cite earlier papers.
Finite-R replicate intervals can be inaccurate for skewed/bimodal replicate laws; a bootstrap-t note concerns the independent RQMC replicate means.
Unbounded/infinite-variation integrands may fail deterministic QMC; RQMC results require their own integrability/singularity assumptions.
sources.proof_status: This author manuscript contains some local proofs (for example ANOVA variance orthogonality and Cranley–Patterson uniformity) but most central discrepancy/scrambled-net results are attributed to external papers/books. Those external proofs are not present in this artifact.
limitations: Many theorem proofs are citations to Owen 1995/1997/2006, Hlawka, Niederreiter, Dick and other sources not separately read.
No universal CLT for randomized nets or general MLQMC complexity theorem is supplied.
The manuscript states: do not distribute or post electronically without the author's permission; it is retained privately in the ignored cache and not quoted.
sources.rights_note: Private author-hosted manuscript. No text is redistributed in the dossier.

checked_local_suppliers.contract: Mutual IID definition; no moment assumption.
Defines sample means without implying independence, common law or integrability.
IID square-integrable mean and exact variance/n Chebyshev weak-law rate.
IID finite mean, strictly positive finite variance; characteristic-function proof.
Almost-sure empirical weak convergence for IID R^d samples using countable compactly supported tests; does not itself imply bootstrap validity.
Bounded-continuous-test definition on metric spaces.
Closed/open-set and continuity-set equivalents.
Weak mapping theorem with a limit-law null-discontinuity condition.
Real-valued distributional convergence plus convergence in probability.
Closed-set Levy–Prokhorov definition.
Metric proof and equivalent open-enlargement convention.
Metrization on separable metric spaces; no completeness needed.
Moment, variance and covariance definitions; no statistical estimator theorem.
Probability, expectation, moments, variance and elementary inequalities.
IID weak law, truncation and independent-series results.
IID, triangular-array and multivariate CLTs; no weak-dependent Hilbert-valued FCLT.
Real-valued convergence modes and Slutsky.
Portmanteau, mapping, weak convergence, Levy–Prokhorov and empirical IID measures.
Relative rounding only in stated normal range; overflow, underflow and invalid operations excluded.
Sequential dot product with nu<1 and all products/intermediate sums normal; componentwise and normwise gamma_n bounds.
Concrete two-term example of the dot-product theorem.
Condition number is a property of an invertible linear-system problem, distinct from algorithm stability.
Conditioning, error, stability and floating-point products; not a generic statistical error-budget theorem.
Backward-stability conclusion is conditional on the displayed local reflector-step perturbation assumptions.
Direct factorization/QR collection; Householder numerical statement retains its local-step hypothesis.
